# Review

Most technical terms are introduced with adequate inline context. "Experience-responsive retention" is defined in the same sentence. "Operative" is glossed as installed and depended on, not merely stored. "Antecedent" is explained as fixed before the development it judges. The two parts of the assessment relation and the prior scope used for non-regression are spelled out in their own sections.

The gaps are at the entry point. The compared object, the software factory, has only a link. The phrase "open production family", which bounds what the claim does not cover, is never explained, but the note's scope disclaimers depend on it.

# Review

## Summary

Most of the body supports the H1. One section argues that the relata are operative states: the predecessor and the installed successor, with no candidate. Another argues that the assessment relation is declared before development and indexed to the predecessor's prior scope. Both parts of the title therefore have support.

The mismatch is in scope. The title is phrased as a general claim about what any better-factory claim does. The body explicitly gives up that generality. It treats *better* as relation-relative and auditable. In its Scope section it says that antecedence is not constitutive of improvement, and that a retrospective criterion can ground a legitimate improvement claim. Read literally, the title asserts something the body denies. A qualifier such as "auditable" would bring the H1 into line with what the body establishes.

# Review

## Summary

The main claim is that a better-factory claim compares two operative states: a predecessor and an installed successor. It uses an assessment relation declared before development. That relation combines non-regression over the predecessor's prior capabilities with a declared improvement. Most side material supports this claim. Several parts stay in place:

- The candidate/successor distinction.
- The whole-production-environment paragraph, which bounds the relata.
- The factory-development preservation consequence, which the description and Scope list tie to the non-regression scope.
- The Scope boundaries.

The retention/improvement/learning section starts as a useful contrast: retention without improvement, and improvement without learning, separate this claim from its neighbours. It then branches into how to establish learning. The with/without-instruction experiment paragraph is about identifying a causal contribution, not about comparing states. It needs different evidence and makes the note more open to attack without strengthening the main claim. That paragraph is the WARN: cut it or move it to the factory-learning note.

A smaller branch on adoption control appears twice. Its destination is unclear, so it gets INFO.

# Review

## Summary

The note's core moves each earn their space. The definitions of predecessor, candidate and operative successor do work. So do the two-component relation, the point that holding model weights fixed does not put the comparison out of reach, and the requirement to preserve a factory-development path. The three hypothetical cases are the clearest way the note separates retention, improvement and learning. Their closing line, "The declared comparison judges improvement; the experience-to-change link distinguishes learning", turns the cases into a decision rule. It is a permitted restatement.

The redundancy is concentrated in hedges about what the framework does not establish. The note says at least four times that a properly declared comparison need not track real quality: once in the introduction, once at the end of the relation section and twice in Scope. It also separates adoption from the comparison in three places. The Scope section mostly restates boundaries the body has already drawn. It adds two things the body does not say: retrospective criteria can ground a different, legitimate improvement claim, and a relation can be declared that allows obsolete capability to be retired. Those two bullets should stay. The flagged bullets and the non-regression paragraph should be cut or folded as described in the findings.

The roadmap sentence after the opening paragraph ("The comparison names the predecessor and adopted successor…") is borderline. It previews the section structure briefly and is not flagged.

# Review

## Summary

The note is mostly literal. Most of its figurative wording is conventional and precise: "keep the comparison's endpoints straight", "read off a construction event", "out of reach", "blocks" and "guards". These phrases add no unsupported connotations. "Factory" is a defined, linked term, not ornament.

One phrase needs a literal replacement. "Audit-proof" in the Scope section is an idiom. It is ambiguous between "immune to audit" and "guaranteed to pass audit", and neither reading matches the auditability the note establishes. "Auditable" or "antecedently declared" says the intended thing directly. This is a single local instance, so the outcome is WARN.

# Friction check: better-factory claim compares operative states

**Central claim (one sentence):** A claim that a factory got better compares the predecessor state with the installed, depended-on successor state under an assessment relation, non-regression on the predecessor's prior scope plus a declared improvement on a named dimension, fixed before the development it judges.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The properties held at once are: operative-state relata, antecedent declaration, relation-relativity (not a quality verdict), non-regression over prior capabilities, and a declared improvement target. These can coexist. The Scope section keeps the claim consistent by making antecedence an auditability condition rather than a constitutive one, and by making the preserved-development-path consequence conditional on the checked scope. The pressure point is non-regression over an open-ended prior scope. The note leaves it as an open question, not as a contradiction.

## Thinnest joints

The antecedence joint ranks thinnest. The note's distinctive addition to the linked independent-specifiability requirement is prior declaration, and that addition is justified by one mechanism, blocking post-hoc selection. The note's own vocabulary lets candidates and staging evidence exist before the declaration, so the stated timing condition does not secure the information barrier the mechanism needs. The prior-capabilities scope ranks next. Its claimed benefit, explicit failure conditions, depends on enumerability, which the note itself questions. The "different relata" step is a smaller gap: the conclusion is plausible, but the stated reason does not carry it. The two `because` joints that cite linked notes hold, because each asks for only what its premise gives.

## For the human

First specify what "declared while only the predecessor exists" excludes: must declaration precede the construction or staging evaluation of candidates, or only installation?

# Critique: A better-factory claim compares operative states under an antecedent assessment relation

**Note:** kb/theory/a-better-factory-claim-compares-operative-states.md
**Central commitment:** An auditable claim that a factory got better compares the predecessor state with the installed operative successor. It uses an assessment relation, declared before development, that combines non-regression on the predecessor's prior capabilities with a declared improvement on at least one named dimension. Declaring that relation first blocks post-hoc selection of the requirements.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

The opponent is a practitioner from preregistration and research-integrity work, in the tradition of Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn on researcher degrees of freedom and Gelman and Loken on the garden of forking paths. That opponent accepts the note's diagnosis: choosing dimensions and thresholds after seeing the result lets the successor satisfy whatever requirements were chosen. The opponent rejects the remedy as specified. In their view, fixing the *requirements* in advance does not by itself prevent post-hoc selection, because the claim has other free parameters that the note leaves open or opens itself:

1. **The successor endpoint.** The note says that in a continuously revised system "the successor can instead be the operative state at a named measurement boundary". It never says that the boundary must be named in advance. A factory under constant revision moves through many operative states. If the assessor picks the measurement point after seeing the trajectory, they can choose a passing state just as easily as they could choose a passing dimension. Both kinds of freedom have the same effect on selection.
2. **The baseline.** The predecessor is "the factory state current when the comparison is declared." If the assessor chooses when to declare, they choose the baseline. Declaring just after a known regression makes ordinary recovery count as improvement.
3. **The number of declarations.** One antecedent declaration is unbiased only if it is the only one. A factory that runs several declared comparisons, or redeclares after a failure, and reports the one that passes has engaged in post-hoc selection across declarations. Preregistration controls this only together with a commitment to report every registered comparison. The note contains no such commitment.

The opponent concludes that the sentence "Prior declaration prevents that form of post-hoc selection" claims more than the mechanism delivers. The note's main reason for requiring antecedence is that it makes the claim auditable and resistant to selection. Without fixing the endpoint and baseline and committing to report every declaration, that guarantee is incomplete in exactly the case the note calls typical, a continuously revised factory.

The author cannot answer this by pointing to the scope bullets. Those bullets admit that antecedence does not make the dimensions the *right* ones. This objection is different. It says that antecedence as specified does not deliver even the *selection-resistance* the note claims for it.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.**

- The note specifies that the relation is "fixed before the development it judges" and is "declared while only the predecessor exists." This fixes the requirements but says nothing about the successor endpoint or the reporting obligation.
- The first Open Question asks "what the declared comparison must specify about the predecessor's baseline, measurement procedures and comparable conditions." That is the right place for the gap. But it treats baseline and measurement specification as open matters of content. It does not recognize them as further degrees of freedom that can undermine the selection-resistance the note has already asserted.
- The note does well to separate auditability from improvement itself ("Antecedence guards this claim's auditability; it is not constitutive of improvement") and to admit that properly declared dimensions may measure the wrong thing. Those concessions answer the Goodhart and validity objection, which is the obvious alternative attack. They do not answer the selection-leakage objection.
- The note's own text creates the endpoint freedom ("a named measurement boundary") without tying it to the antecedent declaration.

So the claim "relation-relative and auditable" survives in substance, and the operative-state relata stand. The non-regression-plus-target structure also stands, and the note correctly bounds it as one declarable shape among others. What the attack defeats is the unqualified statement that prior declaration of the requirements prevents post-hoc selection.

## Constructive findings

- Make the measurement boundary part of the antecedent declaration: either a named point or a rule that fixes which operative state counts as the successor. Otherwise, state that a boundary chosen after development leaves the claim open to endpoint selection.
- Narrow "Prior declaration prevents that form of post-hoc selection" to selection *within a single declaration*. Alternatively, add the condition that full auditability needs: every declared comparison is reported whatever its outcome, and redeclaration after a failure counts as a new comparison, not a replacement.
- In the definition of the predecessor, or in the first Open Question, note that the declaration time sets the baseline. The baseline is therefore one of the degrees of freedom the antecedent declaration has to constrain, not just a matter of measurement content.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- **Stipulative title.** The third scope bullet admits that a retrospective criterion supplied independently can ground a legitimate improvement claim. The title still says "A better-factory claim compares operative states under an antecedent assessment relation" without qualification. The opening paragraph's "Throughout, *better* means better under the declared relation" signals the restriction, but the title and description read as a claim about better-factory claims in general. Qualifying the title, for example as an *auditable* better-factory claim, would match it to the scope the note defends.
- **Prior-capability scope.** Non-regression is measured against "the predecessor's prior capabilities." For an open production family, that scope may not be enumerable. The second Open Question already flags this, so it is noted here only as a residual risk: without an enumerable scope, the non-regression part of the relation may in practice reduce to whatever regression suite happens to exist.
- **Leftover TODO.** The line "TODO! remove or update to use software house instead of software factory" is still in the body. That is an editorial issue, not an objection to the claim, but it signals that the note's core term may change.

# Premise decomposition: better-factory claims compare operative states

**Register:** claim
**Central commitment (one sentence):** A claim that a software factory got better compares the predecessor state with the installed operative successor under an assessment relation, consisting of non-regression on the predecessor's prior scope plus a declared improvement on a named dimension, fixed before the development it judges, and this claim is distinct from retention and from learning.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment has three load-bearing parts, and each consumes its own premises.

The first part says what is compared: the relata are operative states, not candidates or construction events. Its premises concern which states count, and whether both states can be measured comparably. The relata premise holds. The comparability premises are where the commitment is thinnest. The note treats the whole production environment as the compared state but never states that the predecessor stays measurable under conditions comparable to the successor's. Uncontrolled environment drift can therefore pass for factory improvement.

The second part says how the states are compared: an antecedent, two-component, scope-indexed relation. Its premises are that prior declaration blocks post-hoc selection, that the predecessor's prior scope can be named, and that the two-component shape is adequate as this framework's choice. The shape premise holds because Scope fences it. The antecedence premise holds against the narrow failure it names but leaves multiple-comparison selection and design-anticipating declaration unfenced. The scope premise turns on an unresolved ambiguity between "prior capabilities" and "declared prior capabilities".

The third part separates improvement from retention and learning. Its premises are that retention carries no quality guarantee and that learning needs causal contribution. Both hold in substance; only an overstated symmetry in the retention premise is dented.

The decomposition also checks whether the commitment is universal over better-factory claims or limited to the framework's auditable kind. The note's Scope concedes that a retrospective but independent criterion can ground a legitimate improvement claim. The body's stipulation limits "better" to the declared relation, but the title still reads universally. That gap is the one failure that reaches the commitment itself rather than one premise.

## For the human

Look first at the title-versus-Scope tension: either rescope the title to auditable, antecedently declared better-factory claims, or drop the concession that retrospective independent criteria ground legitimate improvement claims.
